claim: Three classes of taste projection neurons (TPNs) in Drosophila melanogaster are distinguished by their morphology and taste selectivity.
source: Here, we identify three classes of taste projection neurons (TPNs) in Drosophila melanogaster distinguished by their morphology and taste selectivity.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by anatomical data in Figures 1-2 and functional data in Figure 3.

claim: TPNs receive input from gustatory receptor neurons.
source: TPNs receive input from gustatory receptor neurons and respond selectively to sweet or bitter stimuli, demonstrating segregated processing of different taste modalities.
evidence: Supported by GRASP experiments (Figure 2B,C) and anatomical overlap studies (Figure 2A) showing physical proximity and potential synaptic connections.

claim: TPNs respond selectively to sweet or bitter stimuli.
source: TPNs receive input from gustatory receptor neurons and respond selectively to sweet or bitter stimuli, demonstrating segregated processing of different taste modalities.
evidence: Calcium imaging experiments (Figure 3C-E) show TPN1 and TPN2 respond to sucrose while TPN3 responds to bitter compounds.

claim: Activation of TPNs influences innate feeding behavior.
source: Activation of TPNs influences innate feeding behavior, whereas inhibition has little effect, suggesting parallel pathways.
evidence: CsChrimson activation experiments (Figure 5A,B) show TPN activation affects proboscis extension response.

claim: Inhibition of TPNs has little effect on innate feeding behavior, suggesting parallel pathways.
source: Activation of TPNs influences innate feeding behavior, whereas inhibition has little effect, suggesting parallel pathways.
evidence: Shibire-mediated silencing experiments (Figure 5C,D) show minimal effects on proboscis extension response.

claim: Two TPN classes are absolutely required for conditioned taste aversion.
source: Moreover, two TPN classes are absolutely required for conditioned taste aversion, a learned behavior.
evidence: Shibire-mediated silencing of TPN2 and TPN3 (Figures 6C,D) dramatically impairs conditioned taste aversion memory.

claim: The TPNs essential for conditioned aversion project to the superior lateral protocerebrum (SLP).
source: The TPNs essential for conditioned aversion project to the superior lateral protocerebrum (SLP) and convey taste information to mushroom body learning centers.
evidence: Anatomical characterization (Figure 4) shows TPN2 and TPN3 axons terminate in the SLP region.

claim: TPNs convey taste information to mushroom body learning centers.
source: The TPNs essential for conditioned aversion project to the superior lateral protocerebrum (SLP) and convey taste information to mushroom body learning centers.
evidence: Calcium imaging experiments (Figures 8-9) show TPN activation affects PPL1 dopaminergic neurons that provide input to mushroom bodies.

claim: TPN1 has two bilaterally symmetric cell bodies in the metathoracic (hind leg) ganglia.
source: TPN1, marked by R30A08-Gal4, has two bilaterally symmetric cell bodies in the metathoracic (hind leg) ganglia, contralateral dendrites in each leg ganglion, and axons that project from the VNC to terminate in the SEZ (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Anatomical imaging with R30A08-Gal4 driver line shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: TPN1 has contralateral dendrites in each leg ganglion.
source: TPN1, marked by R30A08-Gal4, has two bilaterally symmetric cell bodies in the metathoracic (hind leg) ganglia, contralateral dendrites in each leg ganglion, and axons that project from the VNC to terminate in the SEZ (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Anatomical imaging and DenMark/synaptotagmin staining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: TPN1 axons project from the VNC to terminate in the SEZ.
source: TPN1, marked by R30A08-Gal4, has two bilaterally symmetric cell bodies in the metathoracic (hind leg) ganglia, contralateral dendrites in each leg ganglion, and axons that project from the VNC to terminate in the SEZ (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Anatomical imaging and DenMark/synaptotagmin staining shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TPN2 contains two pairs of bilaterally symmetric cells.
source: TPN2 contains two pairs of bilaterally symmetric cells, labeled by VT57358-Gal4.
evidence: Anatomical imaging with VT57358-Gal4 driver line shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: One pair of TPN2 cells has cell bodies on the dorsal surface of the metathoracic neuromere with contralateral VNC dendrites.
source: One pair has cell bodies on the dorsal surface of the metathoracic neuromere with contralateral VNC dendrites and the second pair has cell bodies in the abdominal ganglion with bilateral VNC dendrites (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Single-cell mosaic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The second pair of TPN2 cells has cell bodies in the abdominal ganglion with bilateral VNC dendrites.
source: One pair has cell bodies on the dorsal surface of the metathoracic neuromere with contralateral VNC dendrites and the second pair has cell bodies in the abdominal ganglion with bilateral VNC dendrites (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Single-cell mosaic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The two pairs of TPN2 cells have similar axonal projections in the SEZ and lateral protocerebrum.
source: Otherwise, the two pairs have similar axonal projections in the SEZ and lateral protocerebrum (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Two-cell mosaic and DenMark/synaptotagmin staining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: TPN3 has one pair of cell bodies in the cervical connective.
source: TPN3 has one pair of cell bodies in the cervical connective, bilateral dendrites in the SEZ, and bilateral axonal termini in the lateral protocerebrum (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Anatomical imaging shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F-I.

claim: TPN3 has bilateral dendrites in the SEZ.
source: TPN3 has one pair of cell bodies in the cervical connective, bilateral dendrites in the SEZ, and bilateral axonal termini in the lateral protocerebrum (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: DenMark/synaptotagmin staining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: TPN3 has bilateral axonal termini in the lateral protocerebrum.
source: TPN3 has one pair of cell bodies in the cervical connective, bilateral dendrites in the SEZ, and bilateral axonal termini in the lateral protocerebrum (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Anatomical imaging and DenMark/synaptotagmin staining shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: The dendrites of TPN1 and TPN2 overlapped specifically with sweet GRN axons in the VNC.
source: We found that the dendrites of TPN1 and TPN2 overlapped specifically with sweet GRN axons in the VNC, but not bitter, pheromone, or water GRN axons.
evidence: Double labeling experiments shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The dendrites of TPN1 and TPN2 did not overlap with bitter, pheromone, or water GRN axons.
source: We found that the dendrites of TPN1 and TPN2 overlapped specifically with sweet GRN axons in the VNC, but not bitter, pheromone, or water GRN axons.
evidence: Double labeling experiments shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The dendrites of TPN3 overlapped specifically with bitter GRNs in the SEZ.
source: Conversely, the dendrites of TPN3 overlapped specifically with bitter GRNs in the SEZ, but not sugar, pheromone or water GRN axons (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Double labeling experiments shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The dendrites of TPN3 did not overlap with sugar, pheromone or water GRN axons.
source: Conversely, the dendrites of TPN3 overlapped specifically with bitter GRNs in the SEZ, but not sugar, pheromone or water GRN axons (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Double labeling experiments shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was significant GRASP signal between TPN1/TPN2 and sugar GRNs in the VNC.
source: There was significant GRASP signal between TPN1/TPN2 and sugar GRNs in the VNC, suggesting a direct connection between leg sugar GRNs and both TPN1 and TPN2.
evidence: GRASP experiments shown in Figure 2B,C with quantification.

claim: Strong GRASP signal was found between TPN3 and bitter GRNs in the SEZ.
source: In addition, strong GRASP signal was found between TPN3 and bitter GRNs in the SEZ, both in the anterior ring-like structure (from the labellar bitter GRNs) and the posterior V-like structure (from the leg bitter GRNs) (Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: GRASP experiments shown in Figure 2B,C with quantification.

claim: Limited signal was detected between TPN1/TPN2 and bitter GRNs or TPN3 and sugar GRNs.
source: Limited signal was detected between TPN1/TPN2 and bitter GRNs or TPN3 and sugar GRNs, arguing for modality-specific connections between GRNs and TPNs.
evidence: GRASP experiments shown in Figure 2B,C with quantification.

claim: Both TPN1 and TPN2 showed robust responses to sucrose presentation.
source: Both TPN1 and TPN2 showed robust responses to sucrose presentation, but did not respond to water or a mixture of bitter compounds.
evidence: Calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: TPN1 and TPN2 did not respond to water or a mixture of bitter compounds.
source: Both TPN1 and TPN2 showed robust responses to sucrose presentation, but did not respond to water or a mixture of bitter compounds.
evidence: Calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: TPN3 responded to the bitter mixture, but not sucrose or water.
source: TPN3 responded to the bitter mixture, but not sucrose or water (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: Calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: TPN1 and TPN2 responded to dTRPA1-mediated activation of sugar GRNs.
source: Consistent with the responses to taste compounds, TPN1 and TPN2 responded to dTRPA1-mediated activation of sugar GRNs and TPN3 responded to activation of bitter GRNs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Heat-activated dTRPA1 experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: TPN3 responded to dTRPA1-mediated activation of bitter GRNs.
source: Consistent with the responses to taste compounds, TPN1 and TPN2 responded to dTRPA1-mediated activation of sugar GRNs and TPN3 responded to activation of bitter GRNs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Heat-activated dTRPA1 experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: For TPN1 and TPN2, sucrose delivered to the legs but not the proboscis activated these neurons.
source: For TPN1 and TPN2, sucrose delivered to the legs but not the proboscis activated these neurons (Figure 3F).
evidence: Organ-specific calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claim: TPN3 responded to a bitter mixture applied to either the legs or the proboscis.
source: TPN3 responded to a bitter mixture applied to either the legs or the proboscis (Figure 3G).
evidence: Organ-specific calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 3G.

claim: TPN1 axons terminate specifically in the SEZ.
source: TPN1 axons terminate specifically in the SEZ, TPN2 has axonal termini in the SEZ and higher brain, and TPN3 axons terminate exclusively in the higher brain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,E,I).
evidence: DenMark/synaptotagmin staining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TPN2 has axonal termini in the SEZ and higher brain.
source: TPN1 axons terminate specifically in the SEZ, TPN2 has axonal termini in the SEZ and higher brain, and TPN3 axons terminate exclusively in the higher brain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,E,I).
evidence: DenMark/synaptotagmin staining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: TPN3 axons terminate exclusively in the higher brain.
source: TPN1 axons terminate specifically in the SEZ, TPN2 has axonal termini in the SEZ and higher brain, and TPN3 axons terminate exclusively in the higher brain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,E,I).
evidence: DenMark/synaptotagmin staining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Both TPN2 and TPN3 axons run parallel to the olfactory projection neuron lateral antennal lobe tract (lALT).
source: Both TPN2 and TPN3 axons run parallel to the olfactory projection neuron lateral antennal lobe tract (lALT) (Figure 4D,I).
evidence: Co-labeling experiments with olfactory projection neurons shown in Figure 4D,I.

claim: TPN2 and TPN3 axons do not contact the MB.
source: TPN2 and TPN3 axons do not contact the MB (Figure 4A,F), but terminate predominately in the superior lateral protocerebrum (SLP), with a few synapses in and around the LH in close proximity to olfactory projection neuron axons (Figure 4B,G).
evidence: Co-labeling experiments with mushroom bodies shown in Figure 4A,F.

claim: TPN2 and TPN3 terminate predominately in the superior lateral protocerebrum (SLP).
source: TPN2 and TPN3 axons do not contact the MB (Figure 4A,F), but terminate predominately in the superior lateral protocerebrum (SLP), with a few synapses in and around the LH in close proximity to olfactory projection neuron axons (Figure 4B,G).
evidence: Anatomical characterization shown in Figure 4B,G.

claim: TPN2 and TPN3 have a few synapses in and around the LH in close proximity to olfactory projection neuron axons.
source: TPN2 and TPN3 axons do not contact the MB (Figure 4A,F), but terminate predominately in the superior lateral protocerebrum (SLP), with a few synapses in and around the LH in close proximity to olfactory projection neuron axons (Figure 4B,G).
evidence: Co-labeling experiments with olfactory projection neurons shown in Figure 4B,G.

claim: TPN2 has axons terminating anterior to the LH and along the ventral and medial edges of the LH.
source: TPN2 has axons terminating anterior to the LH and along the ventral and medial edges of the LH (Figure 4C).
evidence: Anatomical sections shown in Figure 4C.

claim: TPN3 has axons terminating anterior to the LH, along the medial edge of the LH.
source: TPN3 also has axons terminating anterior to the LH, along the medial edge of the LH (Figure 4H).
evidence: Anatomical sections shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Activation of either TPN1 or TPN2 increased PER in the absence of a taste stimulus.
source: In the absence of a taste stimulus, activation of either TPN1 or TPN2 increased PER, whereas activation of TPN3 did not elicit PER (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: CsChrimson activation experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Activation of TPN3 did not elicit PER in the absence of a taste stimulus.
source: In the absence of a taste stimulus, activation of either TPN1 or TPN2 increased PER, whereas activation of TPN3 did not elicit PER (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: CsChrimson activation experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Activation of TPN1 or TPN2 did not significantly increase PER in the presence of sucrose.
source: Activation of TPN1 or TPN2 did not significantly increase PER in this context.
evidence: CsChrimson activation with sucrose shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Simultaneous activation of TPN3 with sucrose presentation significantly decreased PER.
source: However, simultaneous activation of TPN3 with sucrose presentation significantly decreased PER (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: CsChrimson activation with sucrose shown in Figure 5B.

claim: TPN silencing did not affect PER to a moderately appetitive stimulus (100 mM sucrose).
source: We found that TPN silencing did not affect PER to a moderately appetitive stimulus (100 mM sucrose) (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Shibire-mediated silencing experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Flies exposed to a bitter-sweet mixture evoked low PER in controls (6–11%).
source: When exposed to a bitter-sweet mixture that evoked low PER in controls (6–11%), flies with synaptic output blocked in TPNs generally showed no change in PER rate (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Shibire-mediated silencing experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Flies with synaptic output blocked in TPNs generally showed no change in PER rate to bitter-sweet mixture.
source: When exposed to a bitter-sweet mixture that evoked low PER in controls (6–11%), flies with synaptic output blocked in TPNs generally showed no change in PER rate (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Shibire-mediated silencing experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Blocking synaptic transmission in TPN1 throughout the entire experiment did not affect aversive taste conditioning.
source: Blocking synaptic transmission in TPN1 throughout the entire experiment with Shits did not affect aversive taste conditioning (Figure 6B), arguing that TPN1, which terminates in the SEZ, is not required for conditioned taste aversion.
evidence: Shibire-mediated silencing during learning assay shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Inhibiting either sugar-responsive TPN2 or bitter-responsive TPN3 throughout the experiment led to a substantial loss of conditioned taste aversion.
source: Surprisingly, inhibiting either sugar-responsive TPN2 or bitter-responsive TPN3 throughout the experiment led to a substantial loss of conditioned taste aversion (Figure 6C,D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Shibire-mediated silencing during learning assay shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Flies presented with sugar as the CS and red-light mediated activation of TPN3 as the US retained an aversive memory that persisted for at least 15 min.
source: Indeed, flies presented with sugar as the CS and red-light mediated activation of TPN3 as the US retained an aversive memory that persisted for at least 15 min.
evidence: CsChrimson-mediated learning assay shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Silencing TPN3 during the pairing phase substantially disrupted memory formation.
source: Indeed, silencing TPN3 during the pairing phase substantially disrupted memory formation while silencing during the testing phase had no effect.
evidence: Phase-specific Shibire silencing shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: Silencing TPN3 during the testing phase had no effect on memory.
source: Indeed, silencing TPN3 during the pairing phase substantially disrupted memory formation while silencing during the testing phase had no effect.
evidence: Phase-specific Shibire silencing shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Silencing TPN2 during testing or training led to strongly impaired conditioned taste aversion.
source: Consistent with this notion, silencing TPN2 during testing or training led to strongly impaired conditioned taste aversion (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Phase-specific Shibire silencing shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Red light activation of TPN3 drove strong calcium responses in most PPL1 neurons.
source: Red light activation of TPN3 drove strong calcium responses in most PPL1 neurons (Figure 8B–D, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B, Figure 9), demonstrating that TPN3 provides an excitatory drive onto PPL1.
evidence: Calcium imaging of PPL1 neurons during TPN3 activation shown in Figures 8 and 9.

claim: TPN2 activation significantly decreased PPL1 calcium levels.
source: We therefore monitored activity in PPL1 neurons while activating TPN2 with CsChrimson and found that TPN2 activation significantly decreased PPL1 calcium levels (Figure 8B–D and Figure 9).
evidence: Calcium imaging of PPL1 neurons during TPN2 activation shown in Figures 8 and 9.

claim: Post-nerve resection, red-light activation of bitter GRNs no longer elicited calcium responses from TPN3.
source: Post-nerve resection, red-light activation of bitter GRNs no longer elicited calcium responses from TPN3 (Figure 10C,G).
evidence: Laser ablation experiments with calcium imaging shown in Figure 10C,G.

claim: Responses in PPL1-MV1 neurons were significantly reduced in magnitude after TPN3 nerve resection.
source: In addition, responses in PPL1-MV1 neurons were significantly reduced in magnitude (Figure 10D,H).
evidence: Laser ablation experiments with calcium imaging shown in Figure 10D,H.

claim: 'Mock' laser ablations to the antennal lobe did not cause significant changes in calcium signals for either TPN3 or PPL1-MV1.
source: Importantly, these results are not due to non-specific effects of laser treatment, as 'mock' laser ablations to the antennal lobe did not cause significant changes in calcium signals for either TPN3 or PPL1-MV1 (Figure 10B,E,F,I,J).
evidence: Mock ablation control experiments shown in Figure 10B,E,F,I,J.

claim: The gustatory system has evolved as a specialized sensory system to detect non-volatile chemicals in the environment.
source: In most animals, the gustatory system has evolved as a specialized sensory system to detect non-volatile chemicals in the environment.
evidence: This is a general statement about gustatory systems based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The taste system innately drives strong food acceptance or rejection behaviors.
source: The taste system innately drives strong food acceptance or rejection behaviors.
evidence: This is a general statement about taste system function based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Gustatory detection of nutrients can serve as a reward to impart positive valence to previously neutral stimuli.
source: In addition, gustatory detection of nutrients can serve as a reward to impart positive valence to previously neutral stimuli whereas bitter detection can act as a punishment signal.
evidence: This is a general statement about taste-mediated learning based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Bitter detection can act as a punishment signal.
source: In addition, gustatory detection of nutrients can serve as a reward to impart positive valence to previously neutral stimuli whereas bitter detection can act as a punishment signal.
evidence: This is a general statement about taste-mediated learning based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Fly gustatory receptor neurons (GRNs) are located on the proboscis labellum, internal mouthparts, legs, and wings.
source: Fly gustatory receptor neurons (GRNs) are located on the proboscis labellum, internal mouthparts, legs, and wings (Stocker, 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Stocker, 1994.

claim: Different GRNs detect different taste modalities, including, sugar, bitter, water, and pheromones.
source: Different GRNs detect different taste modalities, including, sugar, bitter, water, and pheromones (Cameron et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2010; Liman et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2012; Thistle et al., 2012; Thorne et al., 2004; Toda et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Most sensory neurons on the legs and wings send axons to the ventral nerve cord (VNC).
source: Most sensory neurons on the legs and wings send axons to the ventral nerve cord (VNC), whereas those on the proboscis labellum and mouthparts project to the subesophageal zone (SEZ) of the central brain (Stocker, 1994; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Stocker, 1994 and Wang et al., 2004.

claim: Sensory neurons on the proboscis labellum and mouthparts project to the subesophageal zone (SEZ) of the central brain.
source: Most sensory neurons on the legs and wings send axons to the ventral nerve cord (VNC), whereas those on the proboscis labellum and mouthparts project to the subesophageal zone (SEZ) of the central brain (Stocker, 1994; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Stocker, 1994 and Wang et al., 2004.

claim: Activation of sucrose-responsive taste neurons triggers behavioral subprograms associated with feeding, including inhibition of locomotion, extension of the fly proboscis, and ingestion.
source: Activation of sucrose-responsive taste neurons triggers behavioral subprograms associated with feeding, including inhibition of locomotion, extension of the fly proboscis, and ingestion (Gordon and Scott, 2009; Keene and Masek, 2012; Marella et al., 2006; Thoma et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Activation of bitter-responsive sensory neurons triggers food rejection, including proboscis retraction.
source: In contrast, activation of bitter-responsive sensory neurons triggers food rejection, including proboscis retraction (Keene and Masek, 2012; Marella et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Keene and Masek, 2012 and Marella et al., 2006.

claim: Taste cell activation elicits responses in mushroom body learning circuits for sensory associations.
source: In addition, taste cell activation elicits responses in mushroom body learning circuits for sensory associations (Burke et al., 2012; Kirkhart and Scott, 2015; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: A recent study implicated a pair of neurons that projects from the SEZ to the antennal mechanosensory and motor center (AMMC) as candidate second-order taste neurons.
source: A recent study implicated a pair of neurons that projects from the SEZ to the antennal mechanosensory and motor center (AMMC) as candidate second-order taste neurons. These neurons respond to sugar stimulation of proboscis taste neurons and promote proboscis extension (Kain and Dahanukar, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Kain and Dahanukar, 2015.

claim: A different study identified local SEZ interneurons as candidate second-order neurons that sense sugar detection specifically of mouthpart sensory neurons.
source: A different study identified local SEZ interneurons as candidate second-order neurons that sense sugar detection specifically of mouthpart sensory neurons. Inhibiting activity in these neurons selectively inhibited ingestion, and activating them prolonged ingestion without influencing proboscis extension (Yapici et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Yapici et al., 2016.

claim: The SLP is a convergence zone that provides inputs and outputs to the Drosophila mushroom bodies.
source: The SLP is a convergence zone that provides inputs and outputs to the Drosophila mushroom bodies (Aso et al., 2014; Ito et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Aso et al., 2014 and Ito et al., 1998.

claim: Conditioned taste aversion requires the MBs, a learning center in the fly brain.
source: To test whether TPNs participate in learned behaviors, we examined whether they were necessary for conditioned taste aversion, a taste-driven behavior that requires the MBs, a learning center in the fly brain (Keene and Masek, 2012; Kirkhart and Scott, 2015; Masek and Scott, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The principal cells of the MB are the 2000 Kenyon cells (KCs).
source: The principal cells of the MB are the 2000 Kenyon cells (KCs), which receive olfactory, gustatory, and visual cues as conditioned stimuli (CS) at their dendrites in the calyx region (Davis, 2005; Kirkhart and Scott, 2015; Turner et al., 2008; Vogt et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: KC axons receive reward and punishment signals (US) transmitted via aminergic neurons that segment the MB lobes.
source: KC axons receive reward and punishment signals (US) transmitted via aminergic neurons that segment the MB lobes (Burke et al., 2012; Claridge-Chang et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2012; Mao and Davis, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Pairing of the US with the CS causes a synaptic change such that the CS is now sufficient to drive the US behavior.
source: Pairing of the US with the CS causes a synaptic change such that the CS is now sufficient to drive the US behavior (Hige et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Hige et al., 2015.

claim: The bitter US is likely conveyed by PPL1 dopaminergic neurons, as these neurons encode punishment signals, respond to bitter sensory stimulation, and are required for conditioned taste aversion.
source: In the conditioned taste aversion paradigm, the bitter US is likely conveyed by PPL1 dopaminergic neurons, as these neurons encode punishment signals, respond to bitter sensory stimulation, and are required for conditioned taste aversion.
evidence: This statement is based on inference from cited literature about PPL1 function.

claim: The sugar CS is likely conveyed via KC dendrites, as tastes activate KC dendrites with sparse modality-specific representations.
source: Similar to olfactory CS, the sugar CS is likely conveyed via KC dendrites, as tastes activate KC dendrites with sparse modality-specific representations (Kirkhart and Scott, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Kirkhart and Scott, 2015.

claim: PAM dopaminergic neurons that respond to sugars and encode reward are not required for conditioned taste aversion.
source: PAM dopaminergic neurons that respond to sugars and encode reward are not required for conditioned taste aversion (Burke et al., 2012; Das et al., 2014; Kirkhart and Scott, 2015; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Large-scale calcium-imaging studies of taste processing in mammals argue for a labeled line model of taste coding.
source: Large-scale calcium-imaging studies of taste processing in mammals argue for a labeled line model of taste coding, in which different taste modalities are processed in segregated streams (Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2011.

claim: Large-scale calcium-imaging studies of taste processing in Drosophila suggest that labeled-line encoding of tastes is likely to be an ancient strategy shared across evolution.
source: Similar large-scale calcium-imaging studies of taste processing in Drosophila suggest that labeled-line encoding of tastes is likely to be an ancient strategy shared across evolution (Harris et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Harris et al., 2015.

claim: Recent studies in Drosophila have identified interneurons as well as motor neurons that respond selectively to sugars.
source: Recent studies in Drosophila have identified interneurons as well as motor neurons that respond selectively to sugars (Flood et al., 2013; Gordon and Scott, 2009; Kain and Dahanukar, 2015; Yapici et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Studies of olfactory projection neurons set the paradigm for sensory processing in the fly brain, with odor representations in the mushroom bodies and lateral horn suggesting segregation of learned and innate pathways.
source: Studies of olfactory projection neurons set the paradigm for sensory processing in the fly brain, with odor representations in the mushroom bodies and lateral horn suggesting segregation of learned and innate pathways (Jefferis et al., 2007; Marin et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Examination of olfactory projection neurons that convey carbon dioxide detection suggested that innate signals for aversion project to the lateral horn and are conveyed to the MBs for context-dependent associations.
source: Examination of olfactory projection neurons that convey carbon dioxide detection suggested that innate signals for aversion project to the lateral horn and are conveyed to the MBs for context-dependent associations (Bräcker et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Bräcker et al., 2013.

claim: Recent studies of thermosensory processing revealed that different classes of thermosensory projection neurons synapse in the MBs and others in the SLP.
source: Recent studies of thermosensory processing revealed that different classes of thermosensory projection neurons synapse in the MBs and others in the SLP (Frank et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Frank et al., 2015 and Liu et al., 2015.

claim: TPN1 may convey sugar detection on the legs to the SEZ or higher brain.
source: These anatomical studies suggest that TPN1 and TPN2 may convey sugar detection on the legs to the SEZ or higher brain whereas TPN3 may convey bitter signals from the legs and proboscis to higher brain.
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical and functional data presented in Figures 1-3.

claim: TPN2 may convey sugar detection on the legs to the SEZ or higher brain.
source: These anatomical studies suggest that TPN1 and TPN2 may convey sugar detection on the legs to the SEZ or higher brain whereas TPN3 may convey bitter signals from the legs and proboscis to higher brain.
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical and functional data presented in Figures 1-3.

claim: TPN3 may convey bitter signals from the legs and proboscis to higher brain.
source: These anatomical studies suggest that TPN1 and TPN2 may convey sugar detection on the legs to the SEZ or higher brain whereas TPN3 may convey bitter signals from the legs and proboscis to higher brain.
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical and functional data presented in Figures 1-3.

claim: TPN2 and TPN3 may participate in learned associations.
source: The SLP is a convergence zone that provides inputs and outputs to the Drosophila mushroom bodies (Aso et al., 2014; Ito et al., 1998). This suggests that TPN2 and TPN3 may participate in learned associations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical projection pattern of TPN2 and TPN3 to the SLP and the known role of SLP in mushroom body function.

claim: TPN1 might participate in innate feeding behaviors.
source: TPN1 conveys taste information from the legs exclusively to the SEZ, whereas TPN2 and TPN3 project to the SLP, suggesting different taste-processing streams. We hypothesized that TPN1 might participate in innate feeding behaviors, as motor neurons that drive proboscis extension and ingestion localize to the SEZ (Gordon and Scott, 2009; Manzo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on anatomical projection pattern and cited literature about SEZ motor neurons.

claim: TPN2 and TPN3 might participate in learned behaviors.
source: As TPN2 and TPN3 arborize in a mushroom body association area, we hypothesized that they might participate in learned behaviors.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on anatomical projection pattern to the SLP.

claim: Neurons that project to the SEZ (TPN1 and TPN2) as well as those that project to protocerebrum (TPN2 and TPN3) can influence SEZ sensorimotor circuits involved in proboscis extension.
source: As activation of sugar-sensing TPN1 and TPN2 promotes PER whereas activation of bitter-sensing TPN3 inhibits PER, these experiments demonstrate that neurons that project to the SEZ (TPN1 and TPN2) as well as those that project to protocerebrum (TPN2 and TPN3) can influence SEZ sensorimotor circuits involved in proboscis extension.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral effects of TPN activation (Figure 5) combined with anatomical data.

claim: Information from the higher brain feeds back onto sensorimotor circuits for PER.
source: Here, we show that activating sugar-sensing TPN1 or TPN2 promotes PER, whereas activating bitter TPN3 inhibits PER. As both TPN2 and TPN3 send axons to the SLP, this suggests that information from the higher brain feeds back onto sensorimotor circuits for PER.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical projections of TPN2 and TPN3 to higher brain and their effects on PER behavior.

claim: TPNs are not essential for proboscis extension and other neurons must contribute to this behavior.
source: These TPNs could be primary components of taste circuits or may play modulatory roles without being essential components of PER circuits themselves. Conditional inhibition of synaptic transmission in TPNs had little or no effect on proboscis extension (Figure 5). These data argue that TPNs are not essential for proboscis extension and other neurons must contribute to this behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of effect of TPN silencing on PER (Figure 5C,D).

claim: TPN2 carries the CS signal in conditioned taste aversion.
source: These behavioral results are most consistent with the notion that TPN2 carries the CS signal and TPN3 encodes the bitter US.
evidence: This is an inference based on the requirement of TPN2 during both training and testing phases (Figure 7A,B).

claim: TPN3 encodes the bitter US in conditioned taste aversion.
source: These behavioral results are most consistent with the notion that TPN2 carries the CS signal and TPN3 encodes the bitter US.
evidence: This is an inference based on the requirement of TPN3 during training but not testing (Figure 7C,D) and the ability of TPN3 activation to substitute for bitter US (Figure 6F).

claim: TPN3 carries the bitter US signal to the PPL1 cluster.
source: We conclude that TPN3 carries bitter US signals to the PPL1 cluster, but additional pathways must exist.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the reduction (but not elimination) of PPL1 responses after TPN3 ablation (Figure 10).

claim: Additional pathways beyond TPN3 carry bitter signals to PPL1.
source: We conclude that TPN3 carries bitter US signals to the PPL1 cluster, but additional pathways must exist.
evidence: This is an inference based on the persistence of some PPL1 responses after TPN3 ablation (Figure 10D,H).

claim: TPN3 provides an excitatory drive onto PPL1.
source: Red light activation of TPN3 drove strong calcium responses in most PPL1 neurons (Figure 8B–D, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B, Figure 9), demonstrating that TPN3 provides an excitatory drive onto PPL1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increase in PPL1 calcium signals upon TPN3 activation (Figures 8-9).

claim: TPN3 activates dopaminergic PPL1 neurons to convey the bitter US signal to the MBs.
source: These results argue that TPN3 activates dopaminergic PPL1 neurons to convey the bitter US signal to the MBs.
evidence: This is an inference based on TPN3 activation of PPL1 (Figures 8-9) and the known role of PPL1 in conveying punishment signals to MBs.

claim: TPN2 and TPN3 can provide an input into MB circuits.
source: Nevertheless, our calcium-imaging data show that TPN2 negatively regulates PPL1 activity, arguing that TPN2 can provide an input into MB circuits, although the significance for conditioned taste aversion behavior is not clear.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effects of TPN2 activation on PPL1 activity (Figures 8-9).

claim: TPNs might provide a copy of sugar acceptance to the SLP that is then modified downstream of MB learning circuits.
source: An additional possibility is that TPN2 might provide a copy of sugar acceptance to the SLP that is then modified downstream of MB learning circuits.
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative mechanism for TPN2 function.

claim: TPNs also send signals to additional neurons that act upstream or downstream of MB circuits.
source: Although our studies clearly show that TPNs influence activity in MB inputs, they do not exclude the possibility that TPNs also send signals to additional neurons that act upstream or downstream of MB circuits.
evidence: This is speculation about additional TPN functions beyond what was directly tested.

claim: Reciprocal and bidirectional interactions between the SLP and MBs are critical for learned associations.
source: This is consistent with the view that reciprocal and bidirectional interactions between the SLP and MBs are critical for learned associations (Aso et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Aso et al., 2014.

claim: The common routing of different sensory modalities to the SLP area suggests that this may be a site of sensory integration or action selection.
source: The common routing of different sensory modalities to the SLP area suggests that this may be a site of sensory integration or action selection.
evidence: This is speculation based on the convergence of multiple sensory pathways to the SLP.

claim: Representations in the SLP may be modified by MB outputs and may feed back onto innate behavioral programs, like proboscis extension.
source: Representations in the SLP may also be modified by MB outputs and may feed back onto innate behavioral programs, like proboscis extension.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional role of the SLP in integrating learned and innate behaviors.

claim: Sensory processing for innate and learned behaviors may be similar across sensory modalities.
source: The observation that the routing of gustatory information shares similarities to olfactory and thermosensory pathways suggests that sensory processing for innate and learned behaviors may be similar across sensory modalities.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of gustatory, olfactory, and thermosensory projection patterns.
